ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
In the first quadrant of a plane rectangular coordinate system, there is a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the plane and directed into the paper, with a magnetic induction strength of $B=5\times10^{-3}\mathrm{T}$. At a distance $d{=}1.2\mathrm{m}$ above the origin $O$, there is a particle source $S$ that can uniformly emit negatively charged particles with a charge-to-mass ratio of $\frac{q}{m}=2\times10^{6}\mathbf{C}/\mathbf{kg}$ in all directions within the first quadrant. A sufficiently long particle collection device is placed on the positive $x$-axis. When particles collide with the collection device, they are immediately absorbed. The collection device can export the charge to maintain electrical neutrality. The interactions between particles and the influence of gravity are negligible. It is known that $\sin48.5^{\circ}=0.75$.

1. How large must the particle velocity $v_{1}$ be when it reaches the collection device?
2. If the particles emitted by the particle source all have a velocity of $v_{2}=8\times10^{3}\mathbf{m}/\mathbf{s}$, what is the minimum time required for the particles to reach the collection device?
3. If the particles emitted by the particle source all have a velocity of $v_{2}=8\times10^{3}\mathbf{m}/\mathbf{s}$, there will be two particles with different directions of motion that can reach the same position on the collection device. What is the length of these positions on the collection device?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: The figure is the first quadrant of a rectangular coordinate system, O is at the origin, the x-axis points to the right and is labeled collection device (collecting device), and the y-axis points upward. The particle source S is located on the y-axis, above the origin O; in the first quadrant, many “×” symbols indicate a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the paper surface and directed inward. At S, multiple velocity directions pointing to the right are drawn, indicating that particles can be emitted in different directions into the first quadrant. Then reason: A negative charge undergoes uniform circular motion in a magnetic field perpendicular to the paper surface and directed inward, and its trajectory bends toward the collection device. The radius R satisfies R=v/[(q/m)B], and the angular velocity omega=(q/m)B. It is known that (q/m)B=2.0×10^6×5.0×10^-3=1.0×10^4 s^-1. 1. To just be able to reach the x-axis from S, the minimum circle radius corresponds to the circular arc just connecting the height difference d, and the limiting case is 2R_min=d, so R_min=d/2=0.6 m. Thus v1=(q/m)BR_min=1.0×10^4×0.6=6.0×10^3 m/s. 2. When v2=8.0×10^3 m/s, R=v2/[(q/m)B]=8000/10000=0.8 m, omega=1.0×10^4 s^-1. The fastest arrival corresponds to the shortest chord length from S to the x-axis, namely the vertical distance d=1.2 m. Let the corresponding central angle be phi, then sin(phi/2)=d/(2R)=1.2/1.6=0.75. From sin48.5°=0.75, phi/2=48.5°, so phi=97°. Therefore t_min=phi/omega=(97π/180)/(1.0×10^4)=(97π/180)×10^-4 s. 3. Still take R=0.8 m. Let a point on the collection device be P=(x,0), and the chord length SP=sqrt(x^2+d^2). For there to exist a circular arc of radius R connecting S and P, SP≤2R is required, so x≤sqrt((2R)^2-d^2)=sqrt(1.6^2-1.2^2)=sqrt(1.12)=2√7/5 m. The interval where two different emission directions can reach the same point is the part where the circular-arc landing-point mapping overlaps; its left end is the position jointly reached by the horizontally emitted trajectory and the limiting steeper emitted trajectory, x0=R sin120°=0.8×√3/2=2√3/5 m. Therefore the length of these positions is x_max-x0=2√7/5-2√3/5=(2/5)(√7-√3) m.
